title: Change a Template Everyone Depends On
scenario: It is 6:48 AM. This messy morning produced exceptions the brief has no section for: a dropped MISO row and a missing WAUE forecast. The deputy wants a Data Notes section added to the template. Adding a section sounds trivial - it is not, because a template is an interface two audiences depend on.
input:
Change request (Deputy Desk Manager, 6:47 AM): "Add a Data Notes section to the brief so exception days are visible to readers."

Current template v1.0.0 (owner: Desk Manager):
# Meridian Morning Market Brief - <day>
Status / Headline / Hub Summary / Operations

Remember: readers scan the same spots daily, and tomorrow's baseline extraction parses the brief by its sections.
instructions: Treat the template as a governed, versioned interface.
Validate to record the change assessment.

questions.prompt: What KIND of change is adding a Data Notes section?

options.text: A cosmetic tweak any run can make on the fly
A governed structure change: version bump plus owner sign-off
A per-day decision - add the section only when exceptions exist

questions.explain: The template is versioned and owned (v1.0.0, Desk Manager). Changing the sections changes the interface every reader and parser depends on - that is a governance act, not a tweak.

questions.prompt: Should Data Notes appear every day, or only on exception days?

options.text: Every day - printing 'none' on quiet days keeps the structure identical across runs
Only on exception days - why waste a line?
Alternate days, to keep readers alert

questions.explain: A section that comes and goes breaks both audiences: readers lose their scanning spot and parsers lose their anchor. 'Data Notes: none' is a feature - it is the quiet-path logging principle, applied to structure.

questions.prompt: Who approves this change, and what version does the template become?

options.text: The deputy who requested it; version stays 1.0.0
Nobody - templates are not code; just edit it

questions.explain: Requesting is not approving - the OWNER signs off on structure changes. An added section on a 1.0.0 template is 1.1.0, same versioning logic as the threshold policy change.

questions.prompt: What must be checked BEFORE the new section ships?

options.text: Whether tomorrow's baseline extraction still finds its sections after the structure changes
Whether the section name sounds professional

questions.explain: The input's last line names the silent consumer: the parser that seeds tomorrow's baseline. Structure changes are exactly like schema changes - additions can still break positional or brittle consumers, so you check them first.

artifactOnPass.preShipCheck: downstream brief parsing (baseline extraction) still works

copilotPrompt: Assess a template change request as change management: classify the change, decide the section's cadence, name the approver and new version, and identify the downstream consumer to check before shipping.
successMessage: Change assessed. The template can evolve without breaking the readers or the parser that depend on it.

intro.heading: Before you judge: templates are interfaces

sections.title: Two audiences, one structure
sections.body: Humans scan the brief by its sections; tomorrow's automation parses it by them. Any structure change is therefore an interface change with two consumer groups - which is why it gets governance, not a quick edit.

sections.title: Constant structure beats clever structure
sections.body: A conditional section optimizes for the writer; a constant section with 'none' optimizes for every reader and parser forever. The quiet-path principle from the routing layer shows up again here, as structure.

sections.title: Additions can still break consumers
sections.body: It feels safe to only ADD. But brittle consumers - a parser expecting Operations to be the last section, a reader's muscle memory - can break on additions too. Interface changes are checked, not assumed safe.

realWorld.soloRebuildPath: You'd keep last issue's brief as a starting template so today's edition follows the same headings and order.

bestFit.how: the brief layout held as a reusable card definition rather than retyped each day
a Jinja template file loaded at run time, versioned alongside the code

takeaway.heading: Template change managed
points: You treated a 'small' template edit as what it is: a versioned interface change with an owner and consumers.
You chose constant structure (Data Notes every day) so quiet days stay provably quiet in the brief itself.
You separated requester from approver - the deputy asks, the owner signs.
You named the pre-ship check: the silent parser that seeds tomorrow's baseline.
The workflow can now evolve its output structure without breaking either audience that depends on it.
